subject: Re: triage redesign — three-state proposal
body:
Hey,

I went back through the telemetry from the last two weeks and I think the three-state model is right, but only if Waiting means "blocked on someone" and not "I'll get to it". Right now people dump newsletters into Waiting and the queue becomes meaningless.

Proposal:
  - Inbox = needs a decision from me
  - Waiting = I'm waiting on a person or a date
  - Later = parked until something changes
  - Done = closed, never see it again

That gives us four lists that are each honest about what they mean. If we ship only three I'll push back, because Done and Later are the two people actually ask about.

Can you look at the keyboard map before Thursday? I left comments inline.

— Dana

subject: Re: triage redesign — three-state proposal
body:
Following up on my own message, which is a bad habit I know.

The thing I keep coming back to: the list is the interface. If the list is wrong the app is wrong, no matter how fast the rendering is. So let's spend the extra week on getting the state model honest.

Also, small thing — when I hit shift-J I expect the range to be inclusive of where I started. Otherwise I have to hold one extra keystroke in my head and that's exactly the kind of friction we're trying to delete.

Thursday works.

— Dana

subject: Design review notes (9/26)
body:
Hi,

Notes from the design review are below. Everything in the "needs a decision" bucket is on you, everything else is on me.

1. The row height is 28px and the sender column truncates at 220px. Dana asked for more room for the subject; I think 260px is the compromise.
2. Key hints are shown inline at the bottom of the list, always, not only on hover. Nobody discovers hover.
3. The accent color is used for exactly one thing: the cursor. Not for links, not for the unread dot. One accent, one meaning.

I also want to kill the rounded corners. Two pixels maximum. This is a mail client for people who triage, not a wellness app.

— Priya

subject: Re: Design review notes (9/26)
body:
Re: corner radius — I found the real problem. It's not that they're rounded, it's that they're rounded *and* shadowed. Pick one. We pick sharp.

One more: the reader pane should be a full-width overlay, not a split view. Bodies with quoted history are unreadable at 400px. Full width, escape to close, cursor position preserved.

— Priya

subject: TLDR: Rust 1.92, a keyboard-driven everything post, and a font controversy
body:
Rust 1.92 (2026-09-24)
  The 2024 edition is now the default for new crates and cargo will warn on projects that still say 2021. Incremental compilation is about 14% faster on the average binary.

Interfaces
  A long, careful argument for making every single interaction available from the keyboard. The author counts 31 interfaces in a week of work and finds 4 that cannot be driven without a mouse.

Fonts
  The maintainers of a popular terminal font have disabled ligatures for the third time. Comment thread is worth it.

Read more: https://tldr.tech/rust/192

subject: TLDR: database indexes, a CLI framework, and reading RFCs for fun
body:
Databases
  A long-running experiment comparing B-tree, LSM and skip-list indexes over five years of a production table. The winner changes depending on write shape, which is either a useful result or an excuse to keep benchmarking.

Tooling
  A CLI framework that generates completions and man pages from annotations. The interesting part is that it also generates a TUI.

Long read
  Someone actually read RFC 9110 and summarised the parts that affect everyday HTTP debugging. It is much better than it sounds.

https://tldr.tech/databases/indexes

subject: TLDR: the state machine post, plus three short links
body:
Featured
  "Every interface is a state machine you forgot to draw." Twelve pages, no code, one diagram per section. The section on transient states is the one worth reading twice.

Also: why undo stacks are surprisingly hard (spoiler: it is not the stack, it is what you do when a mutation is not a pure function of the selection), and a 1,200-line TUI that fits in a single screen.

https://tldr.tech/interfaces/state-machines

subject: answering my own question
body:
I spent two weeks researching a keyboard-first mail client and bought the thing I was trying to build, which is the most predictable outcome available.

Real finding: the hard part was never the list. It was deciding what 'done' means, and being honest that 'I archived it' and 'I dealt with it' are different states and the second one is almost always the truth.

Happy to write this up properly if it's useful. Otherwise I'll stop bothering you.

— Tomas

subject: the two questions you asked in the talk
body:
You asked me after the talk how I'd handle people who never reply to anything. I thought about it for a week.

My answer: they don't need triage, they need a filter. I want a rule that says "anything from people I have never written back to, older than 30 days, goes somewhere I don't look" — and I want it to tell me where it went so I can reverse the rule later.

The second question was harder: do you archive things you're still waiting on? Yes. All the time. It's the only way the top of my list stays honest.

— Yara

subject: Re: the two questions you asked in the talk
body:
One more thought, because you asked the second question in a slightly different way afterwards and it changed my answer.

If archiving is a real state and 'still waiting' is a flag, then the same message can be both — and that breaks the 'exactly one list' rule that makes the whole thing tolerable.

So: exactly one state, no flags. The waiting part is what you did to the message, the archived part is where it lives. I think I was wrong last week and I want to be wrong in public once.

— Yara
